title: 634. Great Leaders Track the Cost of Caution
author: The Business Leader Daily
summary: This installment argues that organizations keep a meticulous record of the ambitious efforts that failed and no record at all of the ideas that died before they were proposed. The second list is longer and invisible, and the piece treats that asymmetry as an incentive problem rather than a discipline problem. A leader who backs an ambitious idea and watches it fail publicly carries that failure into the next review, while a leader who holds the status quo carries nothing, so teams learn to bring the smaller version of the idea and then the smaller version of that. The supporting evidence is McKinsey's economic profit work, which puts a mid-quintile company's odds of reaching the top quintile over a decade at roughly eight percent, rising to seventeen percent with one or two big moves and close to fifty percent with three. The prescription is procedural: ask in the next staff meeting what the team decided not to do, look for the pattern in what never got proposed, notice who has stopped bringing ideas, and audit whether every budget dollar is already committed to work with a known return.
points: The framing device is the missing ledger, since failures announce themselves while unproposed ideas require someone to go looking.
The essay locates the cause in asymmetric personal exposure rather than in organizational caution as a value.
McKinsey's quintile data is used to make standing still measurable, converting a vague safety into declining odds of growth.
Noticing who has stopped bringing ideas is offered as the highest-signal diagnostic, and explicitly not a workload question.
A fully committed budget is reframed as a five-year strategic decision already made by default.
quotes: A business never forgets when a major effort bombs. The new product launch that missed its mark. The star hire that didn’t work out. A transformation effort that never seems to end. Those failures get names and get revisited again and again as reminders.

A leader who backs an ambitious idea and watches it fail in public carries that failure into their next review. A leader who maintains the status quo avoids that risk. Same year, same company, different exposure. Only one of them ends up explaining themself in a performance review.

McKinsey mapped economic profit across thousands of companies and found the middle of the pack is like quicksand (hard to get out of!). A business sitting in those middle quintiles has roughly an 8 percent chance of climbing into the top quintile over a decade.
Then look at your own budget. If every dollar is committed to work with a known return, you have already made a decision about the next five years, whether you meant to or not.

What set successful CEOs apart was not their lack of mistakes but how they handled mistakes and setbacks when they did occur. CEO candidates who talk about a blowup as a failure are half as likely to deliver strong performance as a CEO.” - Elena L. Botelho, Kim R. Powell & Tahl Raz

Now consider what happens when senior executives, or parents, for that matter, state unequivocally that failure is off-limits, that only good results are acceptable. Failures don’t stop. They simply go underground.” - Amy C. Edmondson from Right Kind of Wrong: The Science of Failing Well

Such an approach to mistake making is characteristic of people we call “failure-tolerant leaders”—executives who, through their words and actions, help people overcome their fear of failure and, in the process, create a culture of intelligent risk taking that leads to sustained innovation. These leaders don’t just accept failure; they encourage it.
